prompt: In a line drawing, hydrogens on carbon are left out, but hydrogens on oxygen and nitrogen are always written in. Why the difference?
choices: A carbon's H count is fixed by its four bonds and can be deduced; an O–H can be gained or lost, so it has to be stated
Oxygen and nitrogen form stronger bonds to hydrogen, so those bonds are drawn
Carbon is never bonded to hydrogen in a line drawing
It is arbitrary convention with no chemical reason behind it
explanation: Carbon always makes four bonds, so its hydrogens follow from the lines you can already see and nothing is lost by omitting them. Oxygen and nitrogen change protonation state constantly: R–OH and its alkoxide R–O⁻ differ by exactly that one hydrogen, and that is the difference between a neutral molecule and a nucleophile. Leaving it off would make the drawing ambiguous.
teach: The convention encodes what varies. Anything deducible gets dropped; anything that could genuinely differ gets written. So the first move on any acid-base problem given as a line drawing is to find every O–H and N–H — those are the hydrogens that actually move.

prompt: A line drawing shows a ketone with no dots anywhere on it. How many lone pairs does that carbonyl oxygen really have?
explanation: Oxygen brings six valence electrons. The double bond accounts for two of them, leaving four — two lone pairs. Line drawings omit lone pairs almost always, but the electrons are still there. An ether or alcohol oxygen also has two; an alkoxide O⁻ has three.
teach: Lone pairs are left off line drawings and matter constantly — every curved arrow in a mechanism starts at a lone pair or a bond, so a drawing with none shown offers no visible starting points. Pencil them onto every N, O and halogen before beginning a mechanism problem. Count: lone pairs = (valence electrons − bonds) ÷ 2, taking a double bond as two.
